Specify a difference-in-differences design with a binary outcome

Source: R/did.R
ape_dgp_did.Rd

Describes a difference-in-differences study with one treatment date: a treated and a control group observed before and after the treated group receives the intervention, in one period each by default or in n_pre periods before and n_post periods after. The target is the average treatment effect on the treated (ATT) after treatment, in probability points, pinned with set_att(). The outcome is regressed on the group indicator, period indicators, the treatment indicator (treated group after the treatment date), and any covariates. Under analysis = "index" (default) that regression is a pooled probit or logit and the ATT is the average partial effect of the treatment indicator over the treated post-period observations (Wooldridge, 2023), with a delta-method standard error. Under analysis = "linear" it is a linear probability model fitted by ordinary least squares and the ATT is the coefficient of the treatment indicator, the standard difference-in-differences estimate.

Usage

ape_dgp_did(
  model = c("probit", "logit"),
  baseline,
  gap = 0,
  trend = 0,
  p_treated = 0.5,
  design = c("panel", "cross-sections"),
  rho = 0,
  p_post = NULL,
  trends = c("index", "linear"),
  analysis = c("index", "linear"),
  n_pre = 1,
  n_post = 1,
  subgroup = NULL,
  covariates = list(),
  correlation = NULL,
  signal = 0,
  gamma = NULL,
  n_int = 4e+05,
  seed_int = 20260812L
)

Arguments

model

"probit" (default) or "logit".

baseline

Outcome rate of the control group before treatment, in (0, 1).

gap

Treated-group rate minus control-group rate before treatment (probability points; default 0).

trend

Change in the control-group rate from before to after the treatment date (probability points; default 0).

p_treated

Share of units (or observations) in the treated group.

design

"panel" (default) or "cross-sections".

rho

Panel designs: latent correlation between any two outcomes of a unit, in [0, 1).

p_post

Cross-section designs: share of observations drawn after the treatment date (default n_post / (n_pre + n_post)).

trends

Scale on which the untreated trends are parallel in the simulated world: "index" (default) or "linear".

analysis

The analysis the simulated studies receive: "index" (default; pooled probit/logit, ATT as an average partial effect) or "linear" (linear probability model, ATT as the coefficient of the treatment indicator, robust standard errors).

n_pre, n_post

Number of periods before and after the treatment date (default one each).

subgroup

Optional binary pa_var() splitting both groups into two subgroups, e.g. pa_var("female", "binary", p = 0.4); see the section 'Comparing two subgroups'.

covariates

List of pa_var() objects (may be empty); time-constant.

correlation

NULL, a scalar, or a correlation matrix over (group, covariates), or over (group, subgroup, covariates) when there is a subgroup – Gaussian-copula dependence, as in ape_dgp().

signal, gamma

Nuisance-signal strength or explicit nuisance coefficients, as in ape_dgp().

n_int, seed_int

Size and seed of the deterministic integration draw used for calibration when there are covariates.

Value

An object of class powerape_dgp (route "did"). Pin the effect with set_att(), then use ape_power(), ape_curve(), ape_n(), or ape_mde().

Details

The world is described on the probability scale by three rates: baseline (control group, before), gap (treated minus control, before), and trend (the control group's change from before to after). With several periods the rates are the same in every period before and in every period after the treatment date, and so is the effect. What the treated group's rate would have been after the intervention date without treatment then depends on the scale on which the two groups' untreated trends are parallel, set by trends:

  • "index" (default): parallel on the probit/logit index, the assumption under which the probit/logit analysis identifies the ATT (Wooldridge, 2023; Puhani, 2012).

  • "linear": parallel in probabilities, the assumption under which the linear analysis identifies the ATT. With covariates the rates are parallel on average over each group's covariates.

Each analysis is unbiased only in the world whose scale it assumes. When trends and analysis name the same scale, ape_power() reports power. When they differ, the analysis centres on another number than the ATT: ape_power() and ape_curve() then report a rejection rate together with the mean of the estimates, and ape_n() and ape_mde() refuse the design. With two periods and no covariates the data cannot tell the two scales apart (Wooldridge, 2023), and the same four cell rates imply different effects under each: the printed design shows both readings. The linear analysis always centres on the cross difference of the four rates.

Data structure

design = "panel" follows the same units over all periods (a balanced panel); n in the power functions counts units, and standard errors are clustered by unit. Outcomes of one unit are dependent through a Gaussian copula with latent correlation rho that leaves the marginal rates exact under either link; under probit this is the random-effects probit with rho = Var(c) / (Var(c) + 1). design = "cross-sections" draws independent observations, each after the treatment date with probability p_post and then in one of that block's periods with equal probability; n counts all observations, and se in ape_power() chooses model-based or robust standard errors for the probit/logit analysis.

More than two periods

The analysis includes an indicator for every period but the first and one treatment indicator, so it estimates one effect, not one per period. In a panel the dependence between two outcomes of a unit is the same however far apart the periods are (one shared unit component). That is the favourable case for adding periods: averaging over periods then removes period-specific noise only, and the gain is larger than under dependence that fades with the distance between periods, which this version does not offer. As an example, with rates of .20 and .30 in the control group, .40 and .60 in the treated group and rho = 0.5, two periods on each side instead of one cut the variance of the linear panel estimate to 51%; if the latent correlation halved with every period of distance it would be 71%. Treat the precision bought by extra periods as an upper bound.

Comparing two subgroups

With subgroup, both subgroups are treated in the treated group and the target is the difference between the two subgroups' effects on the treated, in probability points (the estimand of a triple difference that compares, say, the effect on women with the effect on men; Caron, 2025). baseline, gap and trend may then hold two numbers, for the reference subgroup (subgroup = 0) and for subgroup = 1, and set_att() takes the two effects. The probit/logit analysis is fully interacted with the subgroup and the estimate is the difference of the two subgroups' average partial effects of treatment; the linear analysis estimates the coefficient of the subgroup-by- treatment product. Trends are parallel within each subgroup, on the scale trends names. Three things differ from a single effect. The same eight rates imply different subgroup differences on the two scales, and the printed design shows both. A difference of zero in probability points is not a zero interaction coefficient when the subgroups have different rates. And with equal subgroups a difference as large as the effect itself needs about four times the units the effect needs. ape_mde() searches the difference, holding the reference subgroup's effect at its pinned value.

The linear analysis

A linear probability model is heteroskedastic by construction, so its standard errors are always robust and the se argument of the power functions is ignored: HC1 in cross-sections (as Stata's regress, vce(robust)) and clustered by unit in panels (with the small-sample factor of Stata's regress, vce(cluster)). Ordinary least squares has no separation, so no simulated study is discarded for an all-zero or all-one cell; the sparse-cell warning still applies. In a balanced panel a time-constant covariate changes neither the estimate nor its clustered standard error beyond the degrees of freedom (its contribution cancels in each unit's change), so signal buys the linear panel analysis no precision; in cross-sections it does.

Interval coverage in small samples

Under the index analysis the effect on the treated is a nonlinear function of the estimated rates, and its delta-method interval (the one margins reports in Stata for the same model) covers slightly less than its nominal level when the group-by-period cells are small. In the design without covariates the coverage can be computed exactly. For a 95% interval at a true effect of zero, with rates between 25% and 44%, it is 94.0% with 125 observations per cell, 94.5% with 250, 94.7% with 500 and 94.9% with 1,000 under logit (probit is up to 0.2 points closer to 95%): the shortfall halves when the cells double. A detection claim is therefore made for a true zero effect in 6.0% of studies at 125 per cell and in 5.3% at 500, not in 5%. With covariates and in panels the simulated coverage at about 500 per cell is similar (94.4% to 94.7%). The simulated studies use this interval, so the power reported is the power of the analysis a study will run and needs no correction; with small cells, part of it is this excess. The interval of the linear analysis is close to nominal at the same sizes (94.9% to 95.0% for the same rates).

Limits of this version

One treated group, one treatment date, treatment assigned at the unit level, balanced panels. Staggered adoption, effects that differ by period, pre-trend tests, rates that drift within the before or after block, and treatment assigned to whole clusters are not available. All power functions accept these designs, including ape_robust() (which can also vary the scale on which trends are parallel), power_at(), ape_alpha() and power_statement(). Functions that need power stop for a design whose analysis assumes another scale than its world, because its result is a rejection rate. ape_dgp_did_pilot() builds the design from data observed before the treatment date.

References

Caron, L. (2025). Triple difference designs with heterogeneous treatment effects. arXiv:2502.19620.

Puhani, P. A. (2012). The treatment effect, the cross difference, and the interaction term in nonlinear "difference-in-differences" models. Economics Letters, 115(1), 85-87.

Wooldridge, J. M. (2023). Simple approaches to nonlinear difference-in-differences with panel data. The Econometrics Journal, 26(3), C31-C66.

Examples

d <- ape_dgp_did(model = "logit", baseline = 0.20, gap = 0.20,
                 trend = 0.10, rho = 0.4)
d <- set_att(d, target = 0.07)
d
#> powerape DGP -- logit, difference-in-differences (two periods)
#>   data: panel, both periods per unit; rho = 0.40 (latent within-unit correlation); unit-clustered SEs
#>   analysis: pooled logit; ATT = average partial effect of the treatment indicator over treated post-period rows
#>   treated group: 50% of units
#>   covariates: none
#>   untreated trends: parallel on the logit index (the scale the logit analysis assumes)
#>   rates before -> after: control 0.200 -> 0.300; treated 0.400 -> 0.603 (0.533 without treatment)
#>   true ATT pinned at +0.0700 (treatment coefficient = 0.2858)
#>   the same four rates read under linear-parallel trends: +0.1033 (their cross difference)

## the linear probability analysis in a world with linear-parallel trends
dl <- ape_dgp_did(baseline = 0.20, gap = 0.20, trend = 0.10,
                  trends = "linear", analysis = "linear")
set_att(dl, target = 0.10)
#> powerape DGP -- probit, difference-in-differences (two periods)
#>   data: panel, both periods per unit; rho = 0.00 (latent within-unit correlation); unit-clustered SEs
#>   analysis: linear probability model (OLS); ATT = coefficient of the treatment indicator; unit-clustered SEs
#>   treated group: 50% of units
#>   covariates: none
#>   untreated trends: parallel in probabilities (linear; the scale the linear probability analysis assumes)
#>   rates before -> after: control 0.200 -> 0.300; treated 0.400 -> 0.600 (0.500 without treatment)
#>   true ATT pinned at +0.1000 (treatment coefficient = 0.2533)
#>   the same four rates read on the probit index: +0.0745 (covariate-free reading)
